idiom_name: grammar as types (or data cases) + one interpret/eval over a context
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: represent each grammar rule as a type or data case and give every node the same interpret(context) operation; terminals return a value directly, nonterminals recurse into their children and combine the results, and the client builds or receives the tree and calls interpret on its root. Where the language has a closed variant set with compiler-checked matching, the same structure is written as data plus one external evaluator; where it does not, the class-per-rule hierarchy is hand-written. Decide up front whether the grammar is closed (exhaustive matching, new operations per evaluator) or open (node-owner dispatch, extension by new node types), keep the context explicit, and treat parsing as a separate component.
code_sketch:
type Expr = Terminal(value) | Nonterminal(children: Expr[])
interpret(node, context):
    match node:
        Terminal(v)    -> v
        Nonterminal(c) -> combine(interpret(child, context) for child in c)
# client: root = parse(source); result = interpret(root, context)
pitfalls: Letting the same node also tokenise or parse text: representation, parsing and evaluation are three concerns, and mixing them recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
Growing the grammar without a completeness check (no exhaustive match, no sealed set, no final classes): a missing rule then fails at run time on the input that needs it.
Evaluating with ambient global state instead of an explicit context, so results depend on call order and cannot be reproduced in tests.

Wrong move: Re-parse source text inside every node evaluation -> syntax work, diagnostics and caching become coupled to semantics and repeated evaluations pay the parser cost -> instead parse once into an immutable AST and interpret that tree with an explicit context.

Wrong move: Permit unbounded depth and steps for user-authored trees -> recursive walking can exhaust the call stack or consume CPU and memory before producing a result -> instead enforce depth and step budgets and return a typed limit error.

Wrong move: Forward operator or function names to host-language eval -> a small DSL becomes an expression-language injection path -> instead dispatch through a closed, validated operator registry and sandbox untrusted evaluation.
